title: the summit sit
hook: is a snake lying still a different snake from the one that moves?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the forest of the Devi Mahatmya, and the king's question: why can't the mind let go? Did you ask it once, kindly, when an old hurt came back? Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `WHY CAN'T THE MIND LET GO?`

segments.voice: Is a snake lying coiled in the sun a different snake from the one that slides off into the grass? Nobody would say so. Same snake, resting, then moving. That small picture is credited to Sri Ramakrishna, the temple priest of Dakshineswar, and the year used it to open a whole stretch of teaching. Because in the weeks after the Devi Mahatmya, the path stopped telling the goddess's stories for a while and asked what she is. Today's summit sit climbs back to that question: Shakti, as a way of thinking.
screen: `A SNAKE, COILED.` → `THE SAME SNAKE, MOVING.` → `WHAT IS THE GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Shakti means power. The power to act, to make, to move. In the teaching remembered from Ramakrishna, when the divine is thought of as still, beyond all doing, he called it Brahman. When it is thought of as creating, keeping and dissolving the world, he called it Shakti, the Mother. And then the snake: not two things, one thing, seen at rest and seen in motion. Now take that picture to a hymn the year read. The Saundarya Lahari, a long poem to the goddess traditionally credited to Shankara, opens with a startling sentence. In paraphrase: Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create. Without her, the god cannot so much as stir. A hymn of praise that starts by saying the great god can't move a finger on his own. That's the Shakta turn. Power isn't a tool that someone holds. Power is the goddess herself. From up here, look how often the year came back to it. The goddess rising out of the gods' own blazing power in the Devi Mahatmya, every weapon handed over to her. The hymn in the Rig Veda where a goddess speaks for herself: I move with the gods, I bend the bow. The Lalita hymn that names the goddess as Shiva and Shakti in one form. Different texts, different voices, one thread running through them: the world is not dead matter waiting for a spirit. It moves, and the moving is divine. Shakta teachers, and the Shaiva teachers beside them, read that thread in different ways, and they argue about how the two are related. But the thread is there to argue about.
screen: `SHAKTI: POWER, THE POWER TO MOVE.` · `STILL, BRAHMAN. MOVING, THE MOTHER.` · `WITHOUT HER, SHIVA CANNOT STIR.` · `THE MOVING IS DIVINE.` · then, large: `ONE SNAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stillness and movement, together. Sit, and let the body settle until it's mostly still. Then notice what is still moving. The breath, in and out. The pulse, if you can feel it in your hands. Small shifts of balance. Don't stop any of it. Let the stillness and the movement sit in the same body, the way the coiled snake and the moving snake are one snake. If you pray, you can rest in the goddess as that movement. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Shakti as a philosophy, and a snake that is the same snake, still or moving. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, at one still moment, a red light or a kettle that hasn't boiled, notice what is still moving in you. Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Shakta devotees worship the goddess as the power that moves the world, reciting hymns such as the Saundarya Lahari and the Lalita Sahasranama, and calling her simply Mother.
